title: Expert operating skills learning-based intelligent shared control method for a CT-guided percutaneous biopsy robot - Nature Communications
byline: Wang; Shuang; Zhang; Guoliang; Chen; Wei; Han; Wenlong; Yang; Guang-Zhong; Li; Qing Yun; Qu; Jieming; Xie; Le
html:
Abstract

Accurate and minimally invasive percutaneous biopsy is critical for early lung cancer diagnosis, yet conventional manual procedures suffer from repeated radiation exposure, high reliance on doctor expertise, and risk of tissue injury. This study presents a 5 degree-of-freedom robotic system combined with an intelligent shared control framework guided by expert skills learning. Expert skills were modeled using a variational autoencoder–hidden Markov model to segment latent procedural phases, and dynamic motion primitives reconstructed representative expert trajectories. These learned skills were integrated into a phase-adaptive shared controller, enabling online modulation of impedance and trajectory parameters. Both phantom and in vivo porcine experiments validated the system’s feasibility, safety, and accuracy, with animal experiment studies confirming minimal tissue trauma and stable physiological responses. Compared with manual, leader–follower, and admittance control methods, the intelligent shared control substantially reduced force fluctuations and trajectory deviations.

Introduction

Pulmonary nodules are common in respiratory disease, arising from infection, inflammation, neoplasia, and other causes. Notably, malignant nodules is among the deadliest, causing nearly 25% of cancer deaths1,2. In clinical practice, doctors usually obtain tissues of pulmonary nodules through lung puncture biopsy for accurate diagnosis3. However, during traditional percutaneous puncture biopsy, multiple CT scans are usually required, and the puncture operation cannot be synchronized with image guidance in real time. Doctors require extensive training to perform surgeries, which to some extent affects surgical efficiency and quality4. In addition, frequent scanning and puncture not only increase the risk of radiation exposure to patients, but also easily lead to serious complications such as pneumothorax and bleeding during surgery5, which seriously tests the doctor’s experience level.

Compared with manual operation, robot-assisted surgery can significantly reduce the damage during puncture by optimizing mechanical design, image guidance technology and control algorithms, while improving the efficiency and accuracy of surgery6,7. In recent years, image-guided percutaneous interventional robotic systems have become a research hotspot, and many research teams have developed robotic systems to assist or replace doctors in completing treatment8. Innomotion has developed a leader-follower remote control percutaneous biopsy robot system compatible with CT and MR, which uses a 2 degree-of-freedom (DOF) remote center of motion mechanism and a 3-DOF linear motion mechanism9. The CT-guided leader–follower Zerobot developed by Hiraki et al. has 6 DOF and is capable of performing automatic needle insertion10. The leader–follower percutaneous biopsy robot developed by Won et al. consists of three components: the leader robot, the follower robot, and the positioner integrates both optical and CT guidance to achieve more accurate needle positioning11.

Leader-follower percutaneous biopsy robots have demonstrated significant advantages in reducing the workload of doctors and minimizing radiation exposure risks for both doctors and patients12. However, due to the structural differences between robotic systems and the natural manual puncture techniques, prolonged operations may lead to physiological tremors and fatigue in doctors, ultimately compromising surgical outcomes13. Furthermore, studies have shown that the doctor’s operating skills are critical to the therapeutic efficacy of puncture procedures. Novice doctors typically require extensive model-based and clinical training to acquire proficiency in puncture techniques. Human tissues, such as fat, skin, membranes, and organs, exhibit distinctly different impedance characteristics. During transitions between different types of tissues, the contact force exerted by instruments changes accordingly. When transitioning from a stiffer tissue to a softer one, the contact force decreases significantly—a phenomenon medically referred to as breakthrough sensation14. Due to limited experience, novice doctors often struggle to precisely handle abrupt force variations during both manual and robot-assisted puncture procedures, which can compromise surgical safety. Consequently, numerous researchers are devoted to the intelligent development of percutaneous biopsy robots, aiming to transfer expert doctors’ operating skills to robotic systems. This approach aims to enhance the operational efficiency of robots and alleviate doctor fatigue, while leveraging image-guided navigation to enable robots to learn and emulate expert doctors’ behaviors, thereby achieving intelligent and autonomous operation. Among these efforts, the learning and modeling of expert surgical skills represents a critical research direction.

Surgical skill learning was initially applied to the training of novice doctors. A common approach involves repeated practice on anatomical models or simulators to enhance procedural proficiency. With the widespread adoption of surgical robots, the assessment and learning of robot-operating skills (referred to as LFD) gradually became a research hotspot. Both have a significant influence on surgical skills learning and play a crucial role in advancing robotic autonomy and intelligence15,16. The following section summarizes the recent progress in these two aspects. Traditionally, early skills learning for novice doctors has relied on practicing with anatomical models, with evaluations conducted through checklists completed by experienced doctors observing the procedures. Based on these assessments, novice doctors refine their actions and gradually develop their skills. In recent years, advancements in sensor technology have enabled the integration of sensors into doctors’ hands and surgical instruments, allowing for the objective analysis of surgical skills. Kulik et al. implemented electromagnetic tracking systems affixed to the hands of doctors to capture motion trajectories, thereby enabling an objective evaluation of clinical ultrasound examination competencies17. Zhang et al. proposed an image-based approach to derive instrument positional data for the automated assessment of microsurgical suturing performance18. Prior research predominantly relies on unimodal sensing modalities (motion, image or force) data for data acquisition and model development. Nevertheless, surgical manipulations are inherently complex and heterogeneous, shaped by procedural variations and contextual factors within the operative environment, and often exhibit significant temporal and behavioral dynamics. The corresponding surgical expertise encompasses not only explicit knowledge that can be articulated through language or formal rules, but also tacit skills, latent intentions, and accumulated clinical experience that are challenging to capture or quantify through conventional methods. To more holistically model and interpret surgical proficiency, multimodal data fusion emerges as a promising strategy. Liu et al. constructed a vascular simulation platform to capture doctors’ cannulation behaviors, employing functional data analysis of cannulation angle trajectories to facilitate learning of procedural expertise19. Moreover, Zhou et al. integrated multiple sensing technologies, including electromyography, electromagnetic tracking, fiber optic sensing, and accelerometer to conduct both qualitative and quantitative investigations into the operative patterns of vascular interventionists20,21. Wang et al. proposed a multimodal fusion framework that synergistically incorporates muscle activation signals, finger positional data, proximal force, and tactile pressure inputs, thereby enabling accurate identification and skills learning of eight distinct categories of interventional behaviors22,23. These sensor-based approaches for learning natural operation behaviors offer a promising strategy for capturing expert surgical skills. However, they primarily focus on the modeling of motion gestures, and the learned procedural skills have yet to be validated or transferred onto corresponding surgical robotic platforms.

Learning from demonstration (LFD) is considered one of the most effective ways for robots to learn motion and manipulation skills from humans. Motion trajectory-based methods are widely used in LFD. Among them, dynamic motion primitives (DMP), hidden Markov models (HMM), Gaussian mixture models, and probabilistic motion primitives are the most commonly used baseline methods in high-dimensional input skills learning models for robots. Su et al. proposed a method to combine cognitive functions with demonstration skills, using dynamic time warping to process data obtained from demonstrations, and finally establish a model of doctor’s operating skills after multiple demonstrations during surgical procedures24. Zhai et al. introduced a variable impedance learning method for percutaneous puncture surgery. The model acquired relevant skills through human demonstration learning of motion data and surface electromyographic signals of puncture tasks, assisting doctors in completing smooth puncture tasks25. Wu et al. used sparse variational Gaussian processes and coregionalized multi-output Gaussian processes to encode task variability from multiple demonstrations, enabling robots to learn manipulation skills from large-scale, high-dimensional trajectory data26. However, most current research focuses on the improvement of motion models and the variable impedance control strategy of robots. Different from the relatively fixed application scenarios in the industrial field, such as handling, welding, and milling, due to the differences in the stiffness of human physiological tissues and the operating experience of doctors, it is difficult to fully reflect the doctor’s experience by simply learning the motion data generated by doctors operating robots.

Human-robot shared control has emerged as an effective strategy to balance the autonomy of surgical robots and the decision-making abilities of doctors, especially in uncertain and dynamic environments such as clinical settings27,28. In telemedicine robot systems, shared control mechanisms are widely adopted and have various implementation forms. Fu et al. proposed an active-compliant-passive human-robot shared control framework and used a global energy-based execution mechanism and a compliant controller to improve the safety force tracking performance in medical contact scenarios29. Virtual fixture-based shared control methods30,31,32 have been studied to achieve tactile shared control by combining automation and teleoperator skills. Another common approach is to regulate the passivity of the system based on energy tank to achieve rapid switching between autonomous and bilateral teleoperation modes in telerobotic surgery scenarios33,34,35.

Recent advancements have sought to enhance shared control by incorporating doctor skills learning into the control architecture36,37. Instead of relying solely on predefined rules or static thresholds, adaptive shared control approaches adjust robot autonomy levels based on the doctor’s proficiency or the specific phase of the procedure. In the context of percutaneous interventions such as lung puncture, these intelligent shared control systems are especially advantageous, as they can help stabilize needle insertion trajectories and regulate puncture force in real time. The combination of learned surgical skills and adaptive autonomy fosters a more intuitive and safer human–robot collaboration framework suitable for complex, contact-rich tasks in image-guided interventions.

Despite the remarkable progress in image-guided percutaneous biopsy robots, several limitations still hinder their practical clinical application:

  • Lack of intelligent and autonomous insertion mechanisms: most existing image-guided systems primarily focus on improving positioning accuracy through navigation and visual feedback, yet they rely heavily on manual control for the actual needle insertion process. The absence of an adaptive or autonomous insertion mechanism limits operational precision, prolongs procedure duration, and increases dependency on the doctor’s skill level.

  • Insufficient integration of expert skills into robotic control: current leader–follower robotic systems replicate gross manual movements but fail to capture or reproduce the implicit puncture skills and force–motion coordination of experienced doctors. Without encoding these expert behaviors, the robots cannot dynamically adjust insertion parameters based on tissue impedance variations, leading to suboptimal safety and control performance in complex clinical scenarios.

To overcome these limitations, this study introduces an intelligent and expert skill-informed robotic system to enhance puncture precision, safety, and efficiency. The primary contributions of this study are summarized as follows:

  • Development of a 5-DOF CT-compatible lung percutaneous biopsy robot with leader–follower capability, force feedback, and autonomous needle insertion, enabling precise and controllable operation within the CT imaging environment.

  • Proposal of an expert skills learning framework, in which puncture force and position variations when penetrating tissues of different stiffness are encoded to inform adaptive controller activation, capturing the implicit strategies of expert doctors.

  • An intelligent human–robot shared control strategy integrating expert skills was developed to assist doctors in robotic puncture. The effectiveness and safety of this strategy were rigorously validated through both phantom experiments and in vivo porcine studies, demonstrating submillimeter targeting accuracy, reduced insertion force fluctuations, and minimal tissue trauma.

Results

To comprehensively evaluate the proposed CT-guided percutaneous lung biopsy robotic system, we investigated its robotic functionality, control performance, in vivo feasibility, and respiratory motion management. The compact CT-compatible platform provided the positioning, orientation, and active needle-insertion capabilities required for operation within the confined CT gantry. Phantom experiments showed that the proposed expert skill learning-based shared-control strategy improved needle trajectory stability and reduced doctor-induced tremor, abrupt force variations, and post-penetration motion overshoot compared with manual manipulation and leader–follower control. Porcine experiments demonstrated the feasibility of anterior and lateral puncture approaches and supported the targeting capability and biosafety of the robotic procedure, while rabbit experiments further confirmed the control benefits under physiologically relevant conditions. Finally, respiratory motion was characterized in both a respiratory phantom and an in vivo porcine model, and a low-velocity end-expiratory gating strategy was developed to define a relatively stable needle-insertion window and reduce motion-induced targeting uncertainty.

Percutaneous biopsy robot system design and kinematics analysis

The percutaneous biopsy robot system developed in this study mainly consists of two parts: the leader side and the follower side. The follower side includes a CT scanning device, an image acquisition system, and a designed 5-DOF percutaneous biopsy robot, as shown in Fig. 1A. The leader side console includes image monitoring, CT imaging, and force feedback equipment. Doctors can remotely operate the robot outside the operating room to complete the positioning, orientation, and insertion of the needle, completely avoiding CT radiation, as shown in Fig. 1B. Considering the space limitation in the CT cavity (about 250 mm) and the patient’s wearing comfort, the follower robot designed in this study needs to meet the requirements of miniaturization and lightweight. It needs to have five DOF: two translational DOF to achieve puncture needle positioning, two angular DOF to achieve directional adjustment, and one axial needle insertion degree of freedom to meet the needs of remote puncture operations. Figure 1C is the overall structural diagram of the follower robot. The overall size of the follower robot mechanism is 315 × 210 × 225 mm, and the weight is 2 kg. It can be directly fixed on the patient’s body surface and enter the CT cavity. The main structure is made of 3D-printed photosensitive resin material to reduce weight and avoid metal artifacts in CT scanning. The control board and the motor are centrally arranged at the tail of the mechanism to further reduce imaging interference. The four DOF of orientation and positioning are achieved by two layers of improved Core-XY mechanisms. The conveyor belts are arranged up and down to avoid interference; multi-directional driving force is applied by adjusting the rotation direction of the motor. The needle insertion module is controlled by a motor and adopts a gear structure to achieve axial movement of the puncture needle. A six-dimensional force sensor (M3701A, Sunrise Instruments, China) is installed at the end of the puncture needle to monitor the force during the puncture process. In order not to affect the entry process of the puncture needle, the force sensor is installed at the bottom of the needle body and connected to the needle insertion module through a clamp.
